decks.title: Biological Classification — Part 1: Domains, kingdoms and the bacterial cell
goals: List the distinguishing features of the three domains and tabulate the five kingdoms
Draw and label a typical bacterial cell
Classify bacteria by shape, nutrition and respiration, and distinguish Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria

slides.heading: Biological Classification
slides.body_md: Part 1: from three domains and five kingdoms to the structure of a bacterium.

visual.alt: Flow from domains to kingdoms to Monera

slides.narration: Life can be grouped at the largest scale into three domains, and within them into five kingdoms. This part studies the domains and kingdoms, and then looks closely at kingdom Monera, the bacteria.

slides.heading: Three domains of life
slides.body_md: Carl Woese proposed three domains in 1990, 21 years after Whittaker's five kingdoms, using ribosomal RNA sequences.

visual.alt: Table of the three domains with cell type, cell wall and membrane lipids

slides.narration: Woese compared the ribosomal RNA of many organisms and found that archaebacteria form a separate line. Archaea and Bacteria are both prokaryotes, but their cell walls and membrane lipids differ. Eukarya has cells with a true nucleus.

slides.heading: The tree of three domains
slides.body_md: On the ribosomal RNA tree, Archaea are closer to Eukarya than to Bacteria, even though Archaea and Bacteria both lack a nucleus.

slides.narration: The tree has three main branches. Bacteria diverge first. Archaea and Eukarya share a more recent common ancestor. Both bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes, and all protists, fungi, plants and animals belong to Eukarya.

slides.heading: Five kingdoms
slides.body_md: R. H. Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969, using cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition.

rows: Present in some, absent in others

visual.alt: Table of the five kingdoms by cell type, body organisation, cell wall and nutrition

slides.narration: Monera has prokaryotic cells. The other four kingdoms are eukaryotic. Protista are mostly single-celled, while fungi, plants and animals are multicellular. Plants make their own food, fungi absorb food and animals ingest it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: placing three organisms
slides.body_md: Three unknown organisms are described. Place each in a kingdom.
bullets: **X**: single cell, no nuclear membrane, wall of peptidoglycan: prokaryote, so **Monera**.
**Y**: many cells, true nuclei, chitin wall, absorbs food: **Fungi**.
**Z**: single cell with a nucleus and a shell of silica, makes food by photosynthesis: **Protista**.

visual.alt: Worked table placing three organisms in kingdoms

slides.narration: Use the cell type first. If there is no nuclear membrane, the organism is in Monera. Then look at body plan, wall material and nutrition. A chitin wall with absorptive feeding points to fungi, and a single-celled photosynthetic eukaryote is a protist.

slides.narration: Quick check. Look at the nutrition column.

slides.narration: From outside inward: a capsule, a rigid cell wall of peptidoglycan, and the plasma membrane. Inside are the nucleoid, a small ring of DNA called a plasmid, ribosomes and sometimes a mesosome. Pili help attachment and a flagellum helps movement.

slides.heading: Parts of the bacterial cell
slides.body_md: Each part has a job.

rows: Sticky outer layer; protects the cell and helps it stick to surfaces
Rigid layer of peptidoglycan; gives shape and protection
Selectively permeable; may fold inwards as a mesosome
Region with the single circular chromosome; no nuclear membrane
Small circular DNA; may carry genes for antibiotic resistance
Make proteins; smaller than those of eukaryotes
Movement; attachment, and the pili used in gene transfer

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a bacterial cell and their functions

slides.narration: The nucleoid is not enclosed by a membrane. A plasmid is a small extra ring of DNA that can carry useful genes such as resistance to antibiotics. The flagellum moves the cell, while pili help it attach.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how big does it look?
slides.body_md: A bacillus 2 micrometres long is seen under a microscope that magnifies a thousand times. How long does it look, and how much longer is it than a Mycoplasma cell of 0.1 micrometre?
bullets: Apparent length = 2 × 1000 = 2000 micrometres = **2 millimetres**.
Mycoplasma under the same lens: 0.1 × 1000 = **100** micrometres.
Ratio of lengths = 2 ÷ 0.1 = **20**.

visual.alt: Worked table of apparent sizes of a bacillus and a Mycoplasma cell

slides.narration: Multiply the actual length by the magnification. A bacillus of two micrometres looks two millimetres long at a thousand times. A Mycoplasma cell is twenty times shorter than that bacillus, which is why it is called the smallest living cell.

slides.heading: Nutrition and respiration
slides.body_md: Bacteria differ in how they feed and how they respire.

rows: Uses light energy; cyanobacteria, purple sulphur bacteria
Uses energy from inorganic chemicals; nitrifying and sulphur bacteria
Needs ready-made food; saprophytes (decay) and parasites (disease)
Lives with or without oxygen; Escherichia coli

visual.alt: Table of bacterial groups by nutrition and by respiration

slides.narration: Autotrophic bacteria make their own food, either with light or with chemical energy. Heterotrophic bacteria are saprophytes or parasites. For respiration, obligate aerobes need oxygen, obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate it, and facultative anaerobes manage either way.

slides.heading: The Gram staining steps

slides.narration: Stain the smear with crystal violet, then add iodine, then wash with alcohol, and finally add the counterstain safranin. Gram-positive cells stay purple. Gram-negative cells lose the first stain and appear pink.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Three domains (Woese, 1990): Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya; two are prokaryotic.
Five kingdoms (Whittaker, 1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia; only Monera is prokaryotic.
Bacterial cell: capsule, wall, membrane, nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes, flagellum, pili.
Shapes: coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum; nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic; respiration aerobic, anaerobic or facultative.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, purple. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane, pink.

visual.alt: Summary table of the three domains and whether each is prokaryotic

slides.narration: To recap: three domains and five kingdoms organise life. Bacteria have a capsule, a peptidoglycan wall, a nucleoid and plasmids, come in four basic shapes, and are divided into Gram-positive and Gram-negative by their wall.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name **Woese** with the three domains and **Whittaker** with the five kingdoms.
When drawing a bacterial cell, **label** capsule, wall, membrane, nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes and flagellum.
Link **Gram-positive** with a **thick** peptidoglycan layer and the purple stain.
Say that the nucleoid has **no nuclear membrane**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Link each classification to its scientist. Label the parts of a bacterial cell carefully. Remember that Gram-positive cells have a thick wall and stay purple. And say that the nucleoid lacks a nuclear membrane.

slides.heading: Reproduction, extremes and uses
slides.body_md: Part 2: how bacteria multiply, where the toughest ones live, and how people use them.

visual.alt: Flow of the four topics of Part 2

slides.narration: This part covers four things: how bacteria reproduce and exchange genes, the archaebacteria that live in extreme places, the wall-less Mycoplasma, and the many ways in which bacteria help us.

slides.heading: Reproduction in bacteria: definitions
slides.body_md: Only the **meaning** of each term is needed at this level.

rows: A bacterial cell divides into two identical daughter cells; the usual way of increasing in number
Transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another through direct contact
Transfer of bacterial DNA from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage
Uptake of naked DNA from the surroundings by a bacterium

visual.alt: Table defining fission, conjugation, transduction and transformation

slides.narration: Fission makes two identical cells. The other three terms describe ways in which bacteria exchange genes without dividing: conjugation through contact, transduction by a virus, and transformation by taking up free DNA.

slides.heading: Quick check: gene transfer
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about transformation is true or false.
slides.narration: Quick check. Does transformation need a virus?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: growth by fission
slides.body_md: A tub of milk is seeded with 500 curd bacteria, each dividing every 40 minutes. How many bacteria after 4 hours if growth is unchecked?
bullets: 4 hours = 240 minutes, so the number of generations = 240 ÷ 40 = **6**.
Each generation doubles the number: 500 × 2 to the power 6 = **32000**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the number of bacteria every forty minutes for four hours

slides.narration: Count the generations first. Four hours holds six generations of forty minutes. Doubling six times multiplies the number by sixty-four, so five hundred cells become thirty-two thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: doubling
slides.body_md: A culture starts with 300 cells and each divides every 30 minutes. How many cells after 2 hours?
slides.narration: Quick check. First find the number of generations.

slides.heading: Archaebacteria
slides.body_md: Archaebacteria lack peptidoglycan in the cell wall and live where few other cells can.

rows: Marshes, rice-field mud and the gut of ruminants
Very salty lakes and salt pans
Tolerate high temperature and strong acid

visual.alt: Table of three groups of archaebacteria with habitat and feature

slides.narration: Each group is named for its habitat. Methanogens live without oxygen and release methane. Halophiles need very salty water. Thermoacidophiles live in hot, acidic springs. All three have cell walls without peptidoglycan.

slides.heading: Quick check: extreme habitats
slides.body_md: Match each bacterial group with its habitat or feature.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the habitat each name suggests.

slides.heading: Mycoplasma
slides.body_md: Mycoplasma are also known as **pleuropneumonia-like organisms** (PPLO).

rows: Plasma membrane is the outer boundary; shape varies
Cause diseases in plants and animals

visual.alt: Table of the distinctive features of Mycoplasma

slides.narration: Mycoplasma have no cell wall, so they are flexible and can change shape. They are the smallest known living cells, and many survive without oxygen. Some cause disease in plants and animals.

slides.heading: Comparing the groups
slides.body_md: Three kinds of prokaryote, three kinds of wall.

rows: Hosts such as plants and animals

visual.alt: Table comparing eubacteria, archaebacteria and Mycoplasma

slides.narration: Eubacteria have a peptidoglycan wall. Archaebacteria have a wall without peptidoglycan. Mycoplasma have no wall at all, which is why antibiotics that block wall synthesis do not harm them.

slides.heading: Sewage treatment
slides.body_md: Bacteria clean sewage in stages.

visual.alt: Flow of the stages of sewage treatment

slides.narration: After solids are removed, aerobic bacteria in flocs called activated sludge break down the organic matter. The settled sludge goes to a digester, where anaerobic bacteria, including methanogens, digest it and release biogas.

slides.heading: Energy from dung: biogas
slides.body_md: Methanogens make methane, the main gas in **biogas**, from cattle dung and other wastes.

visual.alt: Flow from cattle dung to biogas

slides.narration: Dung mixed with water is placed in a closed tank without oxygen. Different bacteria break it down, and methanogens form methane. The gas serves as fuel for cooking and lighting, and the slurry that remains is a good manure.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: gas from a dung digester
slides.body_md: A small plant yields about 0.04 cubic metre of biogas from each kilogram of dung. How much gas is expected from 25 kilograms and from 60 kilograms?
bullets: 25 × 0.04 = **1** cubic metre.
60 × 0.04 = **2.4** cubic metres.
The yield is an assumed figure for practice; real plants vary.

visual.alt: Worked table of biogas from 25 and 60 kilograms of dung

slides.narration: Multiply the mass of dung by the yield per kilogram. Twenty-five kilograms give one cubic metre, and sixty kilograms give two point four. The yield used here is an assumed value, chosen only for practice.

slides.heading: Quick check: biogas
slides.body_md: How much biogas is expected from 40 kilograms of dung at 0.04 cubic metre per kilogram?
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the mass by the yield.

slides.heading: Antibiotics, curd and cheese
slides.body_md: Many everyday products depend on bacteria.

rows: Soil bacterium that makes a drug against other bacteria
Changes lactose in milk to lactic acid, which sets the milk
Acid and enzymes ripen and set the milk protein
Releases carbon dioxide gas that forms holes

visual.alt: Table of antibiotics, curd and cheese with the bacteria that make them

slides.narration: Streptomyces gives streptomycin. Lactobacillus turns lactose into lactic acid and so sets milk into curd. Cheese is ripened by bacteria, and the large holes of Swiss cheese come from carbon dioxide produced by Propionibacterium.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Fission: one cell divides into two. Conjugation, transduction and transformation transfer DNA (definitions only).
Archaebacteria: methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles; no peptidoglycan.
Mycoplasma (PPLO): no cell wall, smallest cells, can live without oxygen.
Uses: sewage treatment, biogas, antibiotics (Streptomyces), curd (Lactobacillus), cheese (Propionibacterium holes).

visual.alt: Summary table of archaebacteria and Mycoplasma

slides.narration: To recap: bacteria multiply by fission and may exchange genes in three ways. Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats, Mycoplasma lack a wall, and bacteria help us clean sewage, make fuel gas, medicines, curd and cheese.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **definitions only** for conjugation, transduction and transformation.
Pair each archaebacterial group with its **habitat**.
State **three features** of Mycoplasma: no wall, smallest, survives without oxygen.
Name the **organism** with each product: Lactobacillus, Streptomyces, Propionibacterium.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Define the three gene transfer terms without detail. Link each archaebacterial group with its habitat. Give three features of Mycoplasma. And name the bacterium for every product.

notes.title: Biological Classification: Domains, Kingdoms and Monera — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Three domains and five kingdoms
sections.body_md:
**Three domains.** In 1990 **Carl Woese** and his colleagues proposed that living organisms be placed in three domains, mainly on the evidence of **ribosomal RNA** sequences. **Archaea** and **Bacteria** are both **prokaryotic** (no nuclear membrane, no membrane-bound organelles), but they differ in cell wall and membrane lipids: bacterial walls contain **peptidoglycan**, archaeal walls do **not** (some have pseudomurein or protein), and archaeal membrane lipids are **ether-linked** and branched. **Eukarya** have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and include the kingdoms Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. On the ribosomal RNA tree, Archaea share a more recent ancestor with Eukarya than with Bacteria.

**Five kingdoms.** In 1969 **R. H. Whittaker** proposed five kingdoms, using **cell type** (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), **body organisation** (unicellular, multicellular), **mode of nutrition** (autotrophic, absorptive or ingestive) and also reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Kingdom **Monera** (prokaryotes) is divided between the domains Bacteria and Archaea; the other four kingdoms make up Eukarya.

| Kingdom | Cell type | Body | Cell wall | Nutrition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monera | Prokaryotic | Unicellular | Peptidoglycan (absent in Mycoplasma) | Autotrophic and heterotrophic |
| Protista | Eukaryotic | Unicellular | Present in some, absent in others | Autotrophic and heterotrophic |
| Fungi | Eukaryotic | Multicellular (yeast unicellular) | Chitin | Heterotrophic, absorptive |
| Plantae | Eukaryotic | Multicellular, tissues and organs | Cellulose | Autotrophic |
| Animalia | Eukaryotic | Multicellular, tissues and organs | Absent | Heterotrophic, ingestive |

Only **Fungi** and **Animalia** are entirely heterotrophic; Monera, Protista and Plantae include autotrophs.

key_terms.definition_md: The highest category of classification in Woese’s system: Archaea, Bacteria or Eukarya.
An organism whose cells have no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles.
The rigid polymer of sugars and amino acids in the walls of bacteria, absent from archaea.
An organism that makes its own food, and one that depends on ready-made food.

sections.heading: 2. Bacteria: structure, classification and Gram staining
sections.body_md:
**Structure of a typical bacterial cell.** Size is about 1 to 5 micrometres. From outside inwards: a **capsule** (or slime layer) of polysaccharide; the **cell wall** of **peptidoglycan**; the **plasma membrane**, which may fold inwards as a **mesosome** (many modern workers regard mesosomes as artefacts of preparation); and the **cytoplasm** with **70S ribosomes**, storage granules, a **nucleoid** (a single, circular, naked DNA molecule without a nuclear membrane) and small circular **plasmids** that can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance. **Flagella** give movement and **pili (fimbriae)** help in attachment, with sex pili used in the transfer of DNA.

**Classification by shape:** **coccus** (spherical; diplococcus in pairs, streptococcus in chains, staphylococcus in grape-like clusters), **bacillus** (rod), **vibrio** (comma) and **spirillum** (spiral).

**By nutrition:** **photoautotrophs** (cyanobacteria, purple sulphur bacteria), **chemoautotrophs** (nitrifying and sulphur bacteria) and **heterotrophs** (saprophytes and parasites). **By respiration:** **obligate aerobes** need oxygen; **obligate anaerobes** (Clostridium) are killed by it; **facultative anaerobes** (Escherichia coli) live with or without oxygen.

**Gram staining** (Hans Christian Gram, 1884): smear stained with **crystal violet**, then **iodine**, then washed with **alcohol**, then counterstained with **safranin**. **Gram-positive** bacteria have a **thick peptidoglycan layer**, keep the crystal violet and appear **purple** (Staphylococcus, Bacillus). **Gram-negative** bacteria have a **thin peptidoglycan layer inside an outer membrane** with lipopolysaccharide, lose the crystal violet and appear **pink** (Escherichia coli, Vibrio cholerae).

key_terms.definition_md: The region of a bacterial cell holding its circular DNA, with no nuclear membrane.
A small circular DNA molecule outside the nucleoid that can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.
Bacteria with a thick peptidoglycan wall that retain the crystal violet stain and look purple.
Bacteria with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane that lose crystal violet and look pink.

sections.heading: 3. Reproduction in bacteria (definitions), archaebacteria and Mycoplasma
sections.body_md:
**Reproduction and gene transfer** (definitions only):
- **Fission:** a bacterial cell divides into two identical daughter cells, the usual way of increasing in number. A culture of 500 cells with a generation time of 40 minutes reaches 32000 in four hours (six doublings: 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000).
- **Conjugation:** transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another through direct contact.
- **Transduction:** transfer of bacterial DNA from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage.
- **Transformation:** uptake of naked DNA from the surroundings by a bacterium.

**Archaebacteria** have no peptidoglycan in their walls and live mostly in extreme habitats:
- **Methanogens:** strict anaerobes of marshes, rice-field mud and the gut of ruminants; they produce **methane** (biogas).
- **Halophiles:** live in very salty places such as salt lakes and salt pans.
- **Thermoacidophiles:** live in hot, acidic springs.

**Mycoplasma** (also **PPLO**, pleuropneumonia-like organisms) have **no cell wall**, are the **smallest living cells** (about 0.1 micrometre across) and can **survive without oxygen**; their shape varies and they cause diseases in plants and animals. Because they lack a wall, antibiotics that block wall synthesis, such as penicillin, do not harm them.

sections.heading: 4. Economic importance of bacteria
sections.body_md:
- **Sewage treatment:** in the secondary stage, **aerobic bacteria** in flocs called **activated sludge** oxidise organic matter and reduce its oxygen demand. The settled sludge is then digested by **anaerobic bacteria**, including **methanogens**, in a digester, releasing biogas.
- **Energy production (biogas):** in a closed digester without oxygen, **methanogens** produce **methane** from cattle dung and other wastes; the gas is used as fuel and the leftover slurry as manure. (The yield of 0.04 cubic metre per kilogram used in the worked example is an illustrative figure.)
- **Antibiotics:** the soil bacterium *Streptomyces* produces **streptomycin** and other antibiotics.
- **Curd:** **Lactobacillus** converts the milk sugar lactose to **lactic acid**, which curdles the milk protein.
- **Cheese:** bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus set and ripen cheese; **Propionibacterium shermanii** gives off carbon dioxide that forms the **large holes of Swiss cheese**.

key_terms.definition_md: Flocs of aerobic bacteria and other microbes that oxidise organic matter in sewage.
A fuel gas rich in methane produced by methanogens from dung and other organic wastes.
A chemical made by a microbe that kills or checks other microbes, such as streptomycin from Streptomyces.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that archaebacteria have peptidoglycan; they do not.
- Writing that the bacterial nucleoid has a nuclear membrane.
- Mixing up Gram-positive (thick wall, purple) with Gram-negative (thin wall, outer membrane, pink).
- Describing the stages of conjugation, transduction or transformation; only **definitions** are needed.
- Giving only two features of Mycoplasma when three are asked (no wall, smallest cells, survive without oxygen).
- Forgetting the organism: Lactobacillus (curd), Streptomyces (antibiotic), Propionibacterium (cheese holes).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a scientist, a term, a habitat, an organism, a count or a calculation, a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: domains compared; kingdoms tabulated; Gram-positive against Gram-negative; extreme habitats; uses of bacteria.
- 5-mark questions in parts: five kingdoms in a table; a labelled bacterial cell with classification and Gram staining; domains, archaebacteria and Mycoplasma; economic importance.

questions.stem_md: In which year did R. H. Whittaker put forward the five-kingdom scheme of classification?
questions.solution_md: Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969; 1735 is the date of Systema Naturae, 1884 of Gram’s stain and 1990 of the three domains — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which one of the five kingdoms is made up entirely of prokaryotes?
questions.solution_md: Only Monera has cells without a nuclear membrane — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which kingdoms together make up the domain Eukarya?
questions.solution_md: Eukarya includes every eukaryotic kingdom, that is, all except Monera — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A pond organism is a single cell with a nucleus and a glassy shell of silica, and it makes its food by photosynthesis. In which kingdom is it placed?
questions.solution_md: A unicellular eukaryote that photosynthesises belongs to Protista — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly matches a kingdom with the material of its cell wall?
questions.solution_md: Fungal walls are made of chitin; plant walls of cellulose; Monera have peptidoglycan; animal cells have no wall — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Compare the three domains with respect to cell type, the presence of peptidoglycan in the cell wall and the nature of the membrane lipids.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Archaea:** prokaryotic cells; wall **without peptidoglycan**; **ether-linked, branched** membrane lipids.
**Bacteria:** prokaryotic cells; wall **with peptidoglycan**; **ester-linked** lipids.
**Eukarya:** **eukaryotic** cells with a nucleus; no peptidoglycan (walls of cellulose or chitin, or none); ester-linked lipids.

questions.solution_md: Three domains compared.

questions.stem_md: Compare Monera, Protista and Plantae with respect to cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Monera:** prokaryotic; unicellular; autotrophic or heterotrophic.
**Protista:** eukaryotic; mostly unicellular; autotrophic or heterotrophic.
**Plantae:** eukaryotic; multicellular with tissues and organs; autotrophic by photosynthesis.

questions.solution_md: Three kingdoms compared.

(a) Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker and state the year in which they were proposed. [1]
(b) For Monera, Fungi and Animalia state the cell type, the cell wall and the mode of nutrition. [3]
(c) Which one of the five kingdoms is shared between two domains, and which two domains? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia**, proposed by Whittaker in **1969**.

(b) **Monera:** prokaryotic, wall of peptidoglycan (absent in Mycoplasma), autotrophic or heterotrophic. **Fungi:** eukaryotic, wall of chitin, heterotrophic by absorption. **Animalia:** eukaryotic, no cell wall, heterotrophic by ingestion.

(c) **Monera**, whose members are placed in the domains **Bacteria and Archaea**.

questions.solution_md: Five kingdoms; three compared; Monera in two domains.
